blocks.heading: Key Concepts
blocks.html:
• Pancreas: endocrine (islets of Langerhans) + exocrine (digestive enzymes)
  • Beta cells produce insulin (anabolic: lowers glucose, promotes storage)
  • Alpha cells produce glucagon (catabolic: raises glucose)
  • Thyroid: T3/T4 regulate metabolism; TSH from pituitary controls thyroid
  • Adrenal cortex: cortisol (stress response), aldosterone (Na+/K+ balance)
  • Negative feedback loops maintain hormonal homeostasis

blocks.heading: Normal Values
blocks.html:
• Fasting glucose: 70-100 mg/dL (3.9-5.6 mmol/L)
  • HbA1c: <5.7% normal, 5.7-6.4% prediabetes, >6.5% diabetes
  • TSH: 0.4-4.0 mIU/L
  • Free T4: 0.8-1.8 ng/dL
  • Cortisol (AM): 5-25 mcg/dL
  • Calcium: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL

blocks.heading: What the Nurse Must Know
blocks.html:
• Type 1 DM: autoimmune beta cell destruction, insulin-dependent, usually childhood onset
  • Type 2 DM: insulin resistance + progressive beta cell failure, 90% of cases
  • DKA: Type 1, hyperglycemia + ketosis + metabolic acidosis
  • HHS: Type 2, extreme hyperglycemia WITHOUT ketosis, higher mortality
  • Hypothyroidism: Hashimoto thyroiditis (autoimmune) most common cause

blocks.heading: NORMAL FUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Normal glucose homeostasis: insulin and glucagon balanced
  • Normal thyroid hormone production and feedback
  • Normal cortisol diurnal rhythm
  • Normal calcium/phosphate balance (PTH, vitamin D, calcitonin)

blocks.heading: DYSFUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Diabetes: absolute (Type 1) or relative (Type 2) insulin deficiency
  • Hyperglycemia: osmotic diuresis, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance
  • Hypothyroidism: decreased metabolism, myxedema
  • Hyperthyroidism: increased metabolism, thyroid storm
  • Adrenal insufficiency: cortisol deficiency, Addisonian crisis

blocks.heading: ⚠ Risk Factors (Non-Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Family history (DM, thyroid disease)
  • Autoimmune disease (Type 1 DM, Hashimoto, Graves)
  • Age (Type 2 DM risk increases with age)
  • Genetic syndromes

blocks.heading: 💡 Risk Factors (Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Obesity (central adiposity = major Type 2 DM risk)
  • Sedentary lifestyle
  • Poor diet (high sugar, refined carbohydrates)
  • Previous gestational diabetes
  • Chronic corticosteroid use
  • Iodine deficiency (hypothyroidism) or excess (hyperthyroidism)

blocks.heading: 🔥 Complications
blocks.html: Microvascular: retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy • Macrovascular: MI, stroke, peripheral arterial disease • Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) • Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) • Myxedema coma (severe hypothyroidism) • Thyroid storm (severe hyperthyroidism)
NRG Opposite: Hormonal imbalance leads to metabolic dysregulation, organ damage, life-threatening crises

1. Diabetes: insulin deficiency or resistance leads to hyperglycemia

2. Hyperglycemia exceeds renal threshold (180 mg/dL) causing glycosuria

3. Osmotic diuresis: polyuria, dehydration, electrolyte loss

4. Type 1: absent insulin leads to lipolysis and ketogenesis (DKA)

5. Chronic hyperglycemia: glycation damages vessels and nerves

6. Hypothyroidism: decreased T3/T4 slows all metabolic processes

blocks.heading: Key Detail
blocks.html: Type 1 DM: autoimmune destruction of beta cells leads to absolute insulin deficiency. Without insulin, the body cannot use glucose for energy, so it breaks down fat (ketogenesis) and protein (gluconeogenesis). Type 2 DM: peripheral insulin resistance in muscle and liver, combined with progressive beta cell failure. Chronic hyperglycemia causes AGEs (advanced glycation end-products) that damage microvasculature (retina, glomerulus, nerves) and macrovasculature.

blocks.heading: Clinical Result
blocks.html: Acute: DKA (Type 1) - hyperglycemia + ketosis + anion gap metabolic acidosis. HHS (Type 2) - extreme hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL), profound dehydration, no ketosis, altered consciousness. Chronic: retinopathy (blindness), nephropathy (ESRD), neuropathy (foot ulcers, amputation), cardiovascular disease. Hypothyroidism: bradycardia, hypothermia, myxedema, constipation, depression.
NRG Sequencing: Each step leads to the next — understand the cascade to predict S/S and management

blocks.heading: Early / Mild
blocks.html:
• DM: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, unexplained weight loss (Type 1)
  • DM Type 2: often asymptomatic, fatigue, recurrent infections, slow healing
  • Hypothyroidism: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin
  • Hyperthyroidism: heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, anxiety, palpitations

blocks.heading: Severe
blocks.html:
• DKA: Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath, dehydration, altered LOC
  • HHS: profound dehydration, seizures, coma
  • Hypothyroidism: bradycardia, periorbital edema, delayed DTR relaxation
  • Hyperthyroidism: atrial fibrillation, tremor, exophthalmos, goiter
  • Addisonian crisis: hypotension, shock, hyperpigmentation

blocks.heading: DKA: pH <7.30, altered consciousness
blocks.html:
• DKA: pH <7.30, altered consciousness
  • HHS: osmolality >320, seizures, coma
  • Thyroid storm: fever >104F, tachycardia, delirium, heart failure
  • Myxedema coma: hypothermia, hypotension, altered LOC, hypoventilation
  • Addisonian crisis: vascular collapse
  • THIS IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY

blocks.heading: Diagnostic / Assessment Findings
blocks.html:
• Fasting glucose / HbA1c: diagnose and monitor DM
  • Urine ketones: DKA screening
  • ABG: metabolic acidosis in DKA
  • Serum osmolality: HHS diagnosis
  • TSH, free T4: thyroid function
  • Cortisol, ACTH: adrenal function
  • Microalbuminuria: early diabetic nephropathy

blocks.heading: Link Patho to S/S
blocks.html:
Hyperglycemia → Polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue, blurred vision

Ketosis → Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath, metabolic acidosis

Microvascular damage → Retinopathy (vision loss), nephropathy (proteinuria), neuropathy (numbness)

Hypothyroidism → Bradycardia, cold intolerance, constipation, depression, weight gain

Hyperthyroidism → Tachycardia, tremor, heat intolerance, weight loss, anxiety

blocks.heading: Cardiovascular
blocks.html:
• BP (hypotension in DKA, HHS, Addisonian crisis)
  • HR (tachycardia common; bradycardia in hypothyroidism)
  • Orthostatic vitals
  • Peripheral pulses, edema

blocks.heading: Respiratory
blocks.html:
• Respiratory rate and pattern (Kussmaul = deep rapid)
  • Breath odor (fruity = ketones)
  • SpO2
  • Work of breathing

blocks.heading: Neurological
blocks.html:
• Mental status (altered in DKA, HHS, thyroid extremes)
  • Glasgow Coma Scale if altered
  • Deep tendon reflexes (delayed relaxation in hypothyroidism)
  • Tremor (hyperthyroidism)

blocks.heading: Key Laboratory & Diagnostic Tests
rows: Positive in DKA; negative in HHS
pH <7.30 in DKA; normal in HHS
High osmolality in HHS; K+ shifts in DKA

blocks.heading: Priority Actions
blocks.html: DKA/HHS: fluid resuscitation is FIRST priority (corrects dehydration and reduces glucose). Insulin infusion AFTER fluid resuscitation started. Monitor K+ closely (insulin shifts K+ intracellularly). Calculate corrected sodium. Assess for infection trigger (most common precipitant).

blocks.heading: 💊 Pharmacology - Nursing Monitoring
rows: Hypoglycemia risk - always check BS before dosing
Do NOT hold basal insulin in hospital
D5W when glucose <250 to prevent hypoglycemia
Take on empty stomach, same time daily
Agranulocytosis risk - monitor for fever/sore throat
Type 2 DM first-line: improves insulin sensitivity
Hold if eGFR <30, contrast dye, DKA

blocks.heading: DKA/HHS Management Alert
blocks.html: DKA management: 1) Fluids FIRST (NS 1L in first hour), 2) Insulin (0.1 units/kg/hr), 3) K+ replacement (critical - monitor q2h), 4) Bicarbonate ONLY if pH <6.9. NEVER give insulin without verifying K+ first - insulin drives K+ intracellularly and can cause fatal hypokalemia. When glucose <250 mg/dL, add D5W to prevent hypoglycemia while continuing insulin to clear ketones.

blocks.heading: Lifestyle & Patient Education
blocks.html:
• Carbohydrate counting and meal planning
  • Regular blood glucose monitoring
  • Exercise: lowers glucose, improves insulin sensitivity
  • Foot care: daily inspection, proper footwear, podiatry referral
  • Smoking cessation (reduces macrovascular risk)
🚨 Report Immediately: Blood glucose <70 or >400 | Ketoacidosis symptoms | Altered mental status | Severe dehydration | Fever | Non-healing foot ulcer

blocks.heading: Nursing Diagnosis
blocks.html: Deficient fluid volume related to osmotic diuresis secondary to hyperglycemia (DKA) as evidenced by polyuria, dehydration, dry mucous membranes, and orthostatic hypotension

blocks.heading: Goal / Outcome
blocks.html: Patient will achieve euglycemia (glucose 150-200), normal pH (>7.30), and negative ketones within 24 hours of treatment.

blocks.heading: Interventions
blocks.html:
• Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (NS 1L first hour)
  • Regular insulin infusion per protocol
  • Monitor glucose hourly, K+ q2h
  • Switch to D5W when glucose <250
  • Monitor ABG, anion gap, serum osmolality
  • Assess for infection trigger

blocks.heading: Rationale
blocks.html: Fluid resuscitation corrects dehydration and dilutes glucose. Insulin suppresses ketogenesis and lowers glucose. K+ monitoring is critical because insulin shifts K+ intracellularly. D5W prevents hypoglycemia while allowing continued insulin to clear ketones. Anion gap closure indicates DKA resolution.

blocks.heading: Evaluation
blocks.html: Glucose 180. pH 7.36. Anion gap 12. Ketones trace. K+ 3.8. Patient alert and oriented. Transitioning to subcutaneous insulin.
NRG Care Plan Formula: Problem → Goal → Interventions → Rationale → Evaluation

What system is being tested?

Endocrine - glucose homeostasis and thyroid function

What is the priority?

DKA: fluids FIRST, then insulin, monitor K+ closely; Hypothyroidism: levothyroxine

What is unsafe?

Giving insulin without checking K+, holding basal insulin in hospital, missing thyroid storm

What restores function?

Insulin restores glucose utilization; fluids correct dehydration; levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone

blocks.heading: 💡 Key Memory Aids for RENR
blocks.html:
• Fluids FIRST in DKA: NS 1L in first hour BEFORE insulin - prevents rapid osmotic shifts
  • K+ is CRITICAL: Check K+ before insulin - insulin drives K+ intracellularly, can cause fatal hypokalemia
  • DKA vs HHS: DKA: ketones + acidosis (Type 1); HHS: no ketones, extreme glucose >600, higher mortality (Type 2)
  • Basal insulin NEVER hold: Continue long-acting insulin even when NPO - prevents rebound hyperglycemia
  • Thyroid storm: Fever + tachycardia + agitation in hyperthyroid patient = emergency - cooling, PTU, propranolol, iodide
NRG System Focus Formula: Endocrine Disorder leads to Hormonal imbalance causing Metabolic dysregulation. Priority: DKA fluids + insulin + K monitoring OR thyroid hormone replacement

question.stem: A 22-year-old patient with Type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath odor, and a blood glucose of 480 mg/dL. The laboratory results show: pH 7.22, HCO3 12, K+ 5.8, ketones positive. Which nursing intervention is the priority?

options.html: Start a regular insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr immediately
Administer 1 liter of normal saline IV over the first hour
Give IV potassium replacement to correct the elevated K+
Administer sodium bicarbonate to correct the metabolic acidosis

question.rationale: This is diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): pH 7.22, HCO3 12, glucose 480, positive ketones, Kussmaul respirations. The FIRST priority in DKA management is FLUID RESUSCITATION - 1 liter of NS in the first hour. Fluids correct dehydration (from osmotic diuresis), dilute glucose, and improve renal perfusion for ketone clearance. Insulin should NOT be started before fluids are initiated - rapid glucose reduction without fluid replacement can cause cerebral edema. While K+ is 5.8 (elevated), total body potassium is actually DEPLETED - but insulin is not started until fluids are running. Bicarbonate is reserved for pH <6.9.

why.html: Insulin is important but fluids must come FIRST - prevents cerebral edema
Total body K+ is depleted but insulin drives K+ down - wait until urine output established
Bicarbonate only for pH <6.9 - this patient's pH is 7.22
